lessons.title: An Inspector Calls: themes
lessons.summary: Explore the big ideas of Priestley's play, from social responsibility and class to generation, gender and guilt, and learn how to build a theme-based essay with precise evidence.
objectives: I can explain the theme of social responsibility and how the Inspector and Birling represent opposite views.
I can analyse how class and power shape the way characters treat Eva Smith.
I can explain how Priestley uses age and gender to explore who is able to change.
I can identify how guilt, blame and truth are handled in the play's ending.
I can connect several themes in a single well-organised paragraph.

activities.title: Social responsibility: the play's central argument
activities.content:
## Two views of how to live

At its heart, *An Inspector Calls* is a debate between two ideas.

**Birling's view.** Just before the Inspector arrives, Birling tells the young men that community talk is nonsense and that a man should look after himself and his family. This is **individualism**: the belief that people are responsible only for themselves. Birling backs it with the language of business, calling himself hard-headed and practical.

**The Inspector's view.** In his final speech, the Inspector says that we do not live alone, that we are members of one body, and that we are responsible for each other. This is **collective responsibility**, the idea at the centre of Priestley's socialism. He gives it force by pointing to the millions of ordinary people whose lives are shaped by the decisions of the powerful.

**How Priestley stacks the debate.** The doorbell interrupts Birling mid-speech, as if the Inspector has come to answer him. Each character's story then shows a small act of selfishness with a large consequence. By the end, Sheila and Eric have accepted the Inspector's view; their parents cling to Birling's. The final phone call suggests that those who refuse responsibility will simply face the lesson again.

When you write about this theme, treat Birling and the Inspector as **spokesmen** for two opposing philosophies, and show how the play's structure decides the argument in the Inspector's favour.

activities.title: Building a theme paragraph
activities.content:
**Question:** How does Priestley present ideas about responsibility?

A theme paragraph needs: a **point** about the theme, a **precise moment**, a **method**, an **effect**, and a link to **purpose**.

> Priestley presents responsibility as something the Birlings have been trained to avoid. When the Inspector explains that Eva was sacked for asking for a small rise in wages, Birling defends himself with the language of business, insisting it was his duty to keep costs down. The word *duty* is telling: Birling has a strong sense of responsibility, but only towards profit and his own family. Priestley uses this to show that selfishness often disguises itself as good sense. The Inspector's reply, that it might be better to ask for the earth than to take it, reverses Birling's logic and reframes the strike as a modest request. For a 1945 audience rebuilding after war, this contrast made the case for a fairer society in which employers accept obligations to workers.

**Notice:** the paragraph does not just say *Birling is selfish*; it shows how Priestley makes the audience see his selfishness as a **way of thinking** that must be challenged.

question.text: Which pair of characters best represents the two opposing views of responsibility in the play?
question.hint: One gives a speech about looking after yourself; the other says we are all members of one body.
question.explanation: Birling argues for individualism, that a man should look after himself. The Inspector argues for collective responsibility, that we are all responsible for one another. The rest of the play tests which is right.

options.text: Arthur Birling and Inspector Goole
Sheila and Gerald
options.feedback: Their disagreement is about honesty and the engagement, not the philosophy of responsibility itself.

options.text: Eric and Edna
Mrs Birling and Eva Smith
options.feedback: Eva never speaks, so she cannot argue a position.

activities.title: Class and power
activities.content:
## A world divided by class

Edwardian Britain was rigidly divided. The Birlings are wealthy **upper-middle class**; Gerald's family is **upper class** and titled; Eva Smith and Edna are **working class**. Priestley shows how each class boundary allows one group to damage another without ever seeing them as equals.

**Birling and Eva.** As an employer, Birling has total power over his workers' wages. He sacks the strike leaders to set an example. To him Eva is not a person but a cost.

**Sheila and Eva.** As a customer at Milwards, Sheila can get a shop assistant sacked with a single complaint. She uses her family's spending power as a weapon in a moment of pique.

**Gerald, Eric and Eva.** Both young men meet Eva in the Palace bar, a place where wealthy men went looking for women in difficulty. Their money buys access to her body and her gratitude. Neither considers marrying her.

**Mrs Birling and Eva.** As chair of a charity, Mrs Birling decides who deserves help. She is offended by a working-class girl claiming a connection to her family and refuses her, showing that charity from the powerful can be a form of control.

**Priestley's point.** Each Birling uses the power of their class casually, without malice, and that is what makes it dangerous. The Inspector's warning that there are millions of Eva Smiths turns one story into an argument about the whole social system.

question.text: Match each kind of power to the moment in the play where it is used against Eva Smith.
question.hint: Think about who is boss, who is customer, who has money to spend on a woman, and who controls charity.
question.explanation: Birling's power as an employer sacks her. Sheila's power as a wealthy customer gets her dismissed from the shop. Gerald's money and status let him keep her as a mistress. Mrs Birling's role on the charity committee lets her deny Eva help.

pairs.left: Power of an employer over wages
pairs.right: Birling sacks the girls who led the strike
Sheila's complaint gets Eva dismissed from Milwards

pairs.left: Power of money and status over a vulnerable woman
pairs.right: Gerald installs Daisy Renton in a friend's flat as his mistress

pairs.left: Power to decide who deserves charity
pairs.right: Mrs Birling persuades the committee to refuse Eva help

activities.title: Age and gender
activities.content:
## The generations

Priestley divides the family by age, and the division decides who can change. The Inspector remarks that the young are more impressionable, and the play proves him right. **Sheila and Eric** feel guilt, learn and speak out. **Mr and Mrs Birling** feel only embarrassment and fear of scandal. **Gerald**, though young, chooses the older generation's comfort. Priestley wrote for a 1945 audience about to vote in a general election, and his hope was clearly pinned on the young building a fairer post-war world.

## Gender

The play is also sharp about how women were treated in 1912.

- **Eva** is vulnerable precisely because she is a working-class woman: low wages, no vote, no protection from men like Gerald or Eric, and no support when pregnant. Her choices shrink until the only one left is death.
- **Sheila** is expected to be decorative and to ignore her fiancé's behaviour. Birling and Gerald try to shield her from unpleasant facts, and she has to insist on staying to hear the truth.
- **Mrs Birling** has power, but only within the female sphere of charity and manners, and she uses it to police other women.
- The men treat women as **possessions**: Birling calls the ring a good sign for business, Eric and Gerald speak of Eva as a girl to be picked up.

Priestley invites the audience to see that class, gender and age all shape who is heard and who is silenced.

question.text: Complete the sentences about age and gender in the play.

metadata.blanksText: The Inspector observes that the ___ are more impressionable, which is why Sheila and Eric change. Although he is young, ___ sides with the older generation at the end. Eva is especially vulnerable because she is both working class and a ___.

question.hint: The opposite of old; Sheila's fiancé; Eva's sex.
question.explanation: The Inspector says the young are more impressionable. Gerald, despite his age, joins the Birlings in treating the evening as a hoax. Eva's vulnerability comes from being a working-class woman with no money, rights or protection.

activities.title: Guilt, blame and truth
activities.content:
## Who is to blame?

The Inspector never says that any single person killed Eva. Instead he shows a **chain**: each link on its own might be forgivable, but together they destroy her. This is why the family keeps trying to shift blame. Birling says he cannot be responsible for everything that happens to everyone he has employed; Mrs Birling blames the father of the child; Gerald tries to blame the Inspector for faking it.

**Guilt versus shame.** Priestley distinguishes between the two. **Shame** is about being seen: Birling's terror is of a public scandal. **Guilt** is about what you did: Sheila and Eric feel it whether or not anyone finds out. The hoax section of Act Three is designed to separate these responses. Once the family believes there is no evidence, only those who feel real guilt continue to care.

## Truth and the ending

The play asks whether truth depends on who tells it. Gerald argues that if the photograph was different each time, then there was no single Eva. Sheila answers that whether there was one girl or several, the acts were real. Priestley's final phone call settles the argument: the truth arrives whether or not the Birlings accept it.

**The supernatural angle.** Because the Inspector seems to know things before they are said, and because he leaves just before the truth catches up, some read him as a figure of conscience or a visitor from outside time. Priestley leaves it open so the audience must judge for themselves.

activities.title: Connecting themes in one paragraph
activities.content:
Top-band answers show how themes **interlock**. Here is one paragraph on Mrs Birling that connects class, gender, responsibility and generation.

> Priestley uses Mrs Birling to show how class prejudice hides behind the language of duty. As chair of the charity committee she holds real power over desperate women, yet she treats Eva's request as impertinence because a girl of that class dared to use the Birling name. Her refusal is not a failure of feeling so much as a belief that the poor should know their place, and her insistence that she did nothing wrong reveals the older generation's inability to see responsibility as anything beyond personal respectability. The dramatic irony of her demanding punishment for the unknown father, who is her own son, exposes the double standard of a society that judges working-class women harshly while protecting wealthy young men. In a single character, Priestley connects class, gender and age to make the audience see that the injustice done to Eva is systemic, not accidental.

**Techniques used here:** a clear thesis, evidence from two moments, a method (dramatic irony), and an explicit link between three themes.

question.text: True or false: Priestley suggests that if the Inspector was not a real policeman, then the Birlings did nothing wrong.
question.hint: Think about what Sheila and Eric say after the family discovers the Inspector may be a fake, and what happens in the final moments.
question.explanation: False. Sheila and Eric insist that their actions were real whatever the Inspector was, and the final phone call announcing a real death and a real inspector confirms that the truth does not depend on who reveals it. Priestley separates genuine guilt from mere fear of being found out.

options.text: True
False

question.text: Explain how Priestley uses Sheila's treatment of Eva at Milwards to explore the theme of class.
question.hint: Think about what a customer could do to a shop assistant in 1912, why Sheila did it, and what Priestley wants the audience to notice about small acts of power.
question.explanation: As a wealthy customer, Sheila can have a shop assistant dismissed simply by threatening to close the family account. Her motive is trivial jealousy about a dress, which shows how little effort it takes for the rich to damage the poor. Priestley uses the moment to show that class power is often exercised casually, not cruelly, and that this casualness is exactly what makes the system unjust. Sheila's immediate guilt suggests that recognising this power is the first step to using it responsibly.

markScheme.criterion: Explains that Sheila's wealth or status as a customer gives her power over a working-class shop assistant
Notes the triviality of her motive (jealousy, a dress, a bad temper) compared with the consequence
Explains Priestley's point about casual or thoughtless class power, or about Sheila's guilt as a model response

question.text:
How does Priestley present ideas about social responsibility in An Inspector Calls? Write about:

- what different characters believe about responsibility
- how Priestley presents these ideas through the way he writes the play.
question.hint: Contrast Birling's speech with the Inspector's final speech, use the chain of events, show which characters change, and comment on the timing of the doorbell, dramatic irony and the ending.
question.explanation: A strong answer sets out Birling's individualism against the Inspector's collective responsibility, uses the chain of confessions to show how small selfish acts combine, contrasts the responses of the generations, analyses methods such as the interrupting doorbell, dramatic irony and the cyclical ending, and explains Priestley's purpose for a 1945 audience.

markScheme.criterion: Explains Birling's view that people should look after themselves (individualism), with reference to his speech
Explains the Inspector's view of collective responsibility, with reference to his final speech
Uses the chain of events to show how each character contributed to Eva's death
Contrasts the responses of the younger and older generation
Analyses a dramatic method (the doorbell interrupting Birling, dramatic irony, the ending, the Inspector as device)
Explains Priestley's purpose or the message for a 1945 audience

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Social responsibility**: Birling's individualism versus the Inspector's collective responsibility; the structure decides in the Inspector's favour.
- **Class and power**: each Birling uses a different kind of class power against Eva, casually and without malice; Priestley attacks the system, not just individuals.
- **Age**: the young (Sheila, Eric) change; the old (Mr and Mrs Birling) do not; Gerald chooses the old.
- **Gender**: Eva is doubly vulnerable as a working-class woman; women are treated as possessions or shielded from truth.
- **Guilt, blame and truth**: the family shifts blame; Priestley separates guilt from shame; the ending shows truth arrives regardless.
- Strong essays **connect** themes and always link back to **Priestley's purpose** for his 1945 audience.

practiceQuestions.text: Which theme is most directly expressed in the Inspector's final speech about members of one body?
practiceQuestions.hint: The speech is about how people are connected.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The image of one body expresses collective social responsibility: what happens to one person affects everyone.

options.text: Social responsibility
Romantic love
The supernatural
Business and profit

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Priestley presents the older generation as the characters most willing to learn from the Inspector.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about who is relieved when the Inspector turns out to be a fake.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Mr and Mrs Birling refuse to accept responsibility and are delighted when they think the Inspector was a hoax. It is the younger generation, Sheila and Eric, who learn.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: What is the main difference between guilt and shame as Priestley presents them?
practiceQuestions.hint: One depends on being found out; the other does not.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Shame is about how others see you, which is why Birling fears scandal. Guilt is about what you actually did, which is why Sheila and Eric still care after the hoax is discovered.

options.text: Shame depends on being seen by others; guilt is felt regardless of whether anyone finds out
Guilt is felt only by the older generation; shame only by the younger
There is no difference; Priestley uses the words interchangeably
Shame is a legal term and guilt is an emotional one

practiceQuestions.text: Match each theme to the moment that best illustrates it.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about which scene shows generational difference, gender, class prejudice and blame-shifting.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sheila and Eric rejecting the hoax shows the generational divide. Eva's lack of options as a pregnant, unmarried woman shows gender inequality. Mrs Birling's contempt for a girl of that class shows class prejudice. Gerald's argument about the photographs shows blame-shifting.

pairs.right: Sheila and Eric refuse to treat the evening as a hoax
Eva has nowhere to turn once she is pregnant and unmarried
Mrs Birling is offended that a working-class girl used her name
Gerald argues the Inspector may have shown different photographs

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about Birling's philosophy.

metadata.blanksText: Birling's belief that a man should look after himself and his own is a form of ___, which Priestley contrasts with the Inspector's belief in ___ responsibility.

practiceQuestions.hint: A word meaning 'each person for themselves'; a word meaning 'shared by everyone'.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Birling represents individualism; the Inspector represents collective (or social) responsibility.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO of the following show how women are treated as possessions or as people to be protected from the truth?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the ring, and about who tries to send Sheila out of the room.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Birling links the engagement to a business merger, treating Sheila as part of a deal, and the men try to keep Sheila away from the unpleasant details. Sheila's insistence on staying, and Eric's confrontation, are the opposite of this attitude.

options.text: Birling treats Sheila's engagement partly as a useful business alliance with the Crofts
Birling and Gerald try to keep Sheila from hearing unpleasant details
Sheila insists on staying to hear everything the Inspector says
options.feedback: This is Sheila resisting the way women are treated.

options.text: Eric confronts his mother about refusing to help Eva

practiceQuestions.text: Order these steps for writing an effective theme paragraph.
practiceQuestions.hint: Begin with a claim about the theme and end with Priestley's purpose.
practiceQuestions.explanation: State a point about the theme, choose a specific moment, identify the method, explain its effect, and link to what Priestley wanted the audience to understand.
order: Make a clear point about how the theme is presented
Choose a specific moment from the play as evidence
Identify the dramatic or language method Priestley uses
Explain the effect on the audience
Link the point to Priestley's purpose or message

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how Priestley uses Eva Smith to explore the theme of gender inequality in 1912.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about her jobs, the Palace bar, her pregnancy, and the options available to a working-class woman.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Eva's story shows the narrow options for a working-class woman: low-paid factory and shop work with no security, the risk of exploitation by wealthy men in places like the Palace bar, and complete dependence on charity once pregnant and unmarried. Priestley uses her to show that women, especially poor women, had no protection from the decisions of men, and that society judged them for situations men created.

markScheme.criterion: Refers to Eva's insecure, low-paid work or her lack of economic power
Refers to her exploitation by men (Gerald, Eric, the Palace bar) or her vulnerability once pregnant
Explains Priestley's point that society offered women no protection or judged them unfairly

practiceQuestions.text: Why is the Inspector's remark that there are millions of Eva Smiths important to the theme of responsibility?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the difference between one unlucky girl and a whole social system.
practiceQuestions.explanation: By widening Eva into millions, the Inspector turns a single tragedy into a criticism of society as a whole, so the audience cannot dismiss the story as one unfortunate case.

options.text: It turns one girl's story into a criticism of the whole social system, so the audience cannot treat it as a single unlucky case
It proves that the Inspector invented Eva Smith
It shows that Eva was not really important
It suggests that the Birlings are the only guilty family in Brumley

practiceQuestions.text: How does Priestley present the theme of class in An Inspector Calls? Refer to at least two characters and to the writer's methods.
practiceQuestions.hint: Consider Birling as employer, Mrs Birling's committee, Gerald or Eric at the Palace bar, Edna's few lines, and how Priestley makes the audience judge the family.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A good answer shows different forms of class power (employer, customer, charity, sexual exploitation), notes the casual way it is used, refers to Edna or Eva as the working class present or absent on stage, analyses a method such as the Inspector's questioning or dramatic irony, and explains Priestley's purpose in urging a fairer post-war society.

markScheme.criterion: Explains Birling's power as an employer and his attitude to workers' wages
Explains Mrs Birling's class prejudice or her control of charity
Refers to Eva or Edna as representing the working class, or to the Palace bar as a site of exploitation
Analyses a method Priestley uses (the Inspector's questioning, dramatic irony, the unseen Eva, stage directions)
Explains Priestley's purpose or message about class for his audience
